Cultural AI calls for participatory approaches, emphasizing human input over computational metrics. This can enhance the relevance and application of AI in creative fields. The catch: it requires significant collaboration and resources, which might not be available to all.
— via arXiv

item.title: ‘You cannot sue an AI’: Why adoption comes down to people, not platforms
item.description:
Adopting AI effectively relies more on people adjustments than tech installation. Ensuring your team is ready and willing is crucial for successful AI implementation. The catch: many organizations overlook the human element, risking adoption issues.
— via HR Executive

item.title: The case for common sense at work
item.description:
Pushing for common sense at work suggests a break from over-reliance on data and presentations. Urging leaders to balance analytics with intuition may enhance decision quality. The catch: cultural change is required, which can be slow and challenging.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: ‘Did you use AI?’ is the wrong question. Ask ‘What did you use AI for?’
item.description:
When querying AI use, focus on what it's for, not just if it was used. This helps clarify meaningful contributions of AI to work outcomes. The catch: you'll need to foster open discussions, which may take time to implement effectively.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Amtrak’s ‘relaxed’ COVID-era FMLA policy didn’t cover plaintiff’s unexplained absences, judge rules
item.description:
A judge ruled Amtrak's COVID-era FMLA policy didn't cover unexplained absences. It's a reminder to maintain thorough documentation for compliance. The catch: policies may require frequent updates to stay effective and legally sound.
— via HR Dive

item.title: The EU Pay Transparency Directive: Steps to address payroll fragility
item.description:
The EU Pay Transparency Directive is revealing weak spots in payroll systems. It could mean overhauls for many companies to meet these new standards. The catch: this is mostly about the EU, so if you're elsewhere, the impact is indirect for now.
— via HRZone

item.title: From the Editor: Leadership, resilience and the problem(s) with AI
item.description:
An article explores the challenges AI presents to leadership and resilience in HR. It suggests AI is still causing divided opinions among HR leaders. It’s worth noting this comes from a single publication, so it's more a collection of thoughts than a definitive study.
— via HRZone

item.title: Cultural Misalignment in Large Language Models: Detection, Measurement, and Mitigation Through Targeted Fine-Tuning
item.description:
A study on language models finds cultural mismatches in AI outputs. Fixing these biases takes only a few training tweaks. But remember, it's based on predefined data and might not reflect real-world diversity fully.
— via arXiv

item.title: When Teammates Become Competitors
item.description:
Research shows how competition between team members can hurt collaboration. It could change how you think about team dynamics and incentives. It's a study worth pondering, but it's primarily theoretical, based on one professor's perspective.
— via Knowledge at Wharton

item.title: Permanent hiring rises for first time in nearly four years
item.description:
Permanent job hiring is picking up after a long slump. It indicates a potential shift in the job market towards stability. Yet, the backdrop of fewer vacancies means it’s not all rosy.
— via HRreview

item.title: ET Workplace 2035 brings together business, technology and people leaders to decode the workplace of 2035
item.description:
A summit called Workplace 2035 gathered leaders to talk tech and people. The main focus was on how AI affects workforce strategies. It's more of a thought-starter than concrete changes you can make today.
— via ETHRWorld

item.title: Why Better Models Can Create Riskier Systems: Evidence from LLM Agents in Financial Markets
item.description:
A paper argues that better AI models might still boost risk in systems like finance. It warns of too similar AI behaviors causing unexpected issues. But remember, it's based on simulations, not real-world tests yet.
— via arXiv

item.title: What Analytics Reveal About College Football’s Top Teams
item.description:
An analysis of college football teams through data-driven insights hints at more than sports. The same metrics idea could inspire HR on stability and performance. It’s sports-focused, so extracting HR relevance might take a creative leap.
— via Knowledge at Wharton

item.title: Diffusion TV: Experiencing Diffusion Models through Tangible, Embodied Interaction
item.description:
Diffusion TV lets users interact with AI models through an art project. It’s a fun way to experience AI, but its business applications are limited. Think of it as an example of creative tech, not a tool for workplace use.
— via arXiv

item.title: 5 proven ways to turn disinterest into a job offer
item.description:
A post shares tips on making an impression when a job isn't on the table yet. It's about getting noticed by decision-makers even in informal chats. These tips are anecdotal, with no data backing.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: 5 things Freud got right about your brain
item.description:
An article revisits Freud’s neuroscience ideas, finding some are still valid today. It's a mix of history and modern science. Great for theory, but light on direct takeaways for your people strategy.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Is your workplace passing the back-to-school communication test?
item.description:
The back-to-school season exposes communication gaps in offices. Even small issues can reveal deep-seated problems in how we communicate. Keep in mind, this is more about general observations than specific corrections.
— via HRZone

item.title: How friction can spark creativity at work
item.description:
Friction among workers can ignite creativity, according to a psychologist. Embracing different perspectives could spur innovation. But, it’s often easier said than done, as it hinges on company culture.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Annual HR Report: 23 HR Metrics To Include
item.description:
A blog post lists 23 key HR metrics to show HR’s impact. It's a guide for making stakeholders see HR's value clearly. Beware, it might require tweaking to fit your organization's specifics.
— via AIHR

item.title: America’s disposable workforce is growing. It comes with hidden costs
item.description:
America's workforce is seeing more disposable roles as firms seek flexibility. This might save costs, but there's a hidden expense: it’s leaving workers vulnerable and disengaged. Important to note, these findings come from one book and perspective—your context might vary.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: The most powerful network is a diverse one
item.description:
A diverse network isn't just a checkbox—it's a powerhouse for new ideas. By connecting with people from varied backgrounds, you're exposed to different perspectives that can drive innovation. But remember, it's easy to fall into the comfort trap, networking with those similar to you.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Revolutionizing semiconductor fab operations with AI
item.description:
AI in semiconductor fabs could boost productivity and cut costs. By optimizing operations, early adopters could see noticeable improvements. The downside? This insight focuses solely on fabs, so don’t expect overnight wonders in other sectors.
— via McKinsey

item.title: AI transformations run on trust
item.description:
For AI changes to stick, trust is as critical as the tech itself. Leaders must focus on transparency and supporting their teams for real transformation. However, the guidance originates from premium sources, so sift through with a critical eye.
— via McKinsey

item.title: Jean-Christophe Fann - Harvard Business Review
item.description:
More S&P 500 firms are hiring CHROs from outside, not within. Fresh perspectives can invigorate policies, but it might slow employee growth and internal pathways. This insight focuses on large companies—smaller firms might have different trends.
— via HBR

item.title: Marsh: Health benefits costs to see biggest jump in 24 years
item.description:
According to Marsh, the jump is the highest since 2003, and is being driven by a number of factors—from healthcare consolidation to GLP-1s. The post Marsh: Health benefits costs to see biggest jump in 24 years appeared first on HR Executive .
— via HR Executive

item.title: CHROs are increasingly external hires at large companies, index shows
item.description:
AI’s impact on entry-level jobs is overstated; the real shift began when leaders opted out of truly entry-level hiring. AI accelerates a trend that started before the tech boom. It’s a specific perspective—mileage may vary by industry and region.
— via HR Executive

item.title: ReRoom: Blending Virtual and Physical Contexts for In Situ Room Planning in Mixed Reality
item.description:
Planning a real domestic space is an in situ authoring process: users evaluate candidate layouts at true scale, refine their intent, and carry accepted decisions into later iterations. Existing approaches either separate layout editing from the physical room or provide limited support for evaluating and refining whole-room proposals in situ. We present…

item.title: Occlusion-Robust Multimodal Emotion Recognition in VR via Fusion of Facial Images and EMG
item.description:
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) fundamentally limit emotion recognition in virtual reality (VR): by occluding the upper face, they render conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete, particularly for applications requiring real-time affective assessment. We address this challenge by fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG)…
— via arXiv

item.description:
But compensation decisions often “continue well beyond the annual merit cycle,” Marsh said.

I was on my feet most of the day and took pride in inserting my time card into the punch clock machine registering the start of my…

item.title: AI did not kill the entry-level job. Leaders did.
item.description:
The rise of AI has just exacerbated a problem that was already in place but few companies want to talk about. Many companies chose to begin walking away from true entry-level hiring years ago. AI only accelerated it.

item.description:
Unemployment rates are substantially higher and more volatile in the euro area relative to the United States. We ask to what extent the lack of cross-country labor mobility can account for unemployment dynamics in Europe. Our analytical model incorporates downward nominal wage rigidity and an endogenous migration decision. Firms are unable to freely adjust…
— via NBER

item.title: How to set project boundaries as a solopreneur
item.description:
A post on managing project boundaries as a solopreneur offers some valuable lessons. It's a reminder to set clear limits to keep projects from ballooning unexpectedly, saving time and energy. However, this advice mainly applies to individual projects, not complex team settings.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Gen X and millennials feel least positive after work, new research finds
item.description:
New research shows Gen X and millennials feel less positive after work compared to other generations. Understanding this can help tailor engagement strategies to maintain morale. The research is limited to self-reported feelings, which may not capture the full story.
— via HR Executive

item.title: 16 skills that become more valuable because of AI
item.description:
A new article outlines 16 skills that AI makes more valuable. These skills focus on where human judgment outshines machines, elevating their importance in decision-making. It's broad advice and may not apply equally across all industries.
— via Fast Company Work Life

item.title: Another ‘whiplash’ month for the labor market as August beats expectations
item.description:
August showed unexpected resilience in the labor market despite its fragile state. This keeps us on our toes regarding hiring and resource planning. The 'whiplash' nature means conditions can quickly change, so stay updated.
— via HR Dive

item.title: Spot Toxic Leadership Traits in an Interview
item.description:
There's a new post about spotting toxic leadership traits during interviews. This could be game-changing as it helps you avoid future headaches by identifying red flags early. The catch? This research is fresh and from one source, so use it as guidance, not gospel.
— via HBR

item.title: Jean-Christophe Fann - Harvard Business Review
item.description:
Jean-Christophe Fann provides insights on HRIS in a recent HBR article. Understanding HRIS better could revolutionize how you manage personnel data and processes. Remember, it's a single exploration and might not cover all possible systems or nuances.
— via HBR

item.title: 150 Employee Evaluation Examples & Comments for Every Rating
item.description:
AIHR offers 150 employee evaluation examples to replace vague feedback. These can help you provide clearer, actionable feedback, potentially boosting performance. But don't forget, applying them without context could still miss the mark.
— via AIHR

item.title: The power of purpose, culture, and grit: An interview with JoAnne Bass
item.description:
JoAnne Bass discusses the role of purpose, culture, and grit in leadership. These elements are crucial in adapting and succeeding in changing environments. Just remember, these insights come from a particular leadership pathway and might not suit all organizations.
— via McKinsey

item.title: Race bias claims tied to drug test can go to jury, 11th Circuit says
item.description:
A legal case about race bias tied to drug tests is making waves. It highlights the importance of fair employment practices and avoiding discriminatory perceptions. Just note, the details are specific to this case and region, so consider your own context.
— via HR Dive

item.description:
Employers now have a say in shaping the CMS drug cost survey program. This is a chance to influence prescription benefit structures to better align with your cost and care goals. It's specific to those involved in the program, so not everyone will benefit directly.
— via HR Executive

item.title: Psychological capital is a business advantage. Here’s why it matters
item.description:
Psychological capital is emerging as a critical business advantage. Understanding and fostering it can improve employee resilience and engagement. However, the concept requires more tangible measures to track its impact effectively.
— via HR Executive

item.title: Book Briefing: ‘The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work’ by Gleb Tsipursky
item.description:
The book 'The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work' dives into how AI affects employee and manager attitudes. Recognizing these attitudes can help navigate AI implementation smoother. It's based on focused group research, which might not cover every experience.
— via Charter

item.title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
item.description:
A new paper argues for governing AI models, not just data. This impacts how we ensure ethical AI use by focusing on accountability and control. Remember, this is academic insight and may need translation into practical application.
— via arXiv

item.title: Is POSH failing women at work?
item.description:
A piece questions if POSH (Prevention of Sexual Harassment) is failing women at work. This is crucial for ensuring a safe and supportive workplace environment. Still, it's based on specific legal frameworks, so always adapt to your local laws.
— via ETHRWorld

item.title: Company’s inability to explain one manager’s firing over another keeps FMLA claim alive
item.description:
A recent case shows that unclear firing reasons can hold up legal claims like FMLA. Without explanation, comparators in cases may lead to prolonged legal battles. This example highlights the need for clear documentation when making managerial decisions.
— via HR Dive
